planting.note: Set container-grown clumps in consistently moist to boggy, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; this is one of the only palms that tolerates standing water at the roots, making it a good choice along pond edges, rain gardens, or as a low-light houseplant kept evenly damp.

directions: Chamaedorea cataractarum forms a dense, trunkless clump of arching, deep-green pinnate fronds from a mass of suckering stems, spreading gradually into a broad clump rather than growing tall. It is native to streambanks and seasonally flooded forest floors in Mexico, which explains its unusual tolerance for wet feet — soggy or poorly drained soil that would rot most other palms is fine here, and it also handles very low light better than almost any other palm sold for interior use. Keep soil evenly moist, avoid letting it dry out between waterings, and protect from temperatures below the mid-20s F, since cold and drought, not overwatering, are what typically kill it. Its dense, low, spreading habit makes it useful as a shaded groundcover mass or a foundation planting under live oaks where taller palms would look leggy.

planting.note: Plant clumps in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this is among the most cold-tolerant Chamaedorea species, taking brief dips into the upper teens F once established, so it can be tried outdoors a zone or more colder than most parlor-palm relatives.

directions: Native to the mountains of Tamaulipas and Nuevo Leon, Mexico, Chamaedorea microspadix sends up multiple slender, cane-like stems topped with feathery, dark-green pinnate fronds, gradually forming a bamboo-like thicket 6 to 10 feet tall. It is one of the few Chamaedorea species that can survive an occasional hard freeze without dying back to the ground, which makes it a realistic candidate for outdoor zone 8 gardens in a sheltered, shaded courtyard or north-facing bed. Clusters of small orange-red berries follow inconspicuous flowers on female plants when both sexes are grown nearby. Divide congested clumps or simply let new canes fill in over time; it needs little more than consistent shade and occasional feeding to form a dense, textural screen beneath larger trees.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; give this larger clustering species room to spread, as established clumps expand steadily via new canes and can eventually form a substantial thicket.

directions: Chamaedorea costaricana is a clustering understory palm from the cloud forests of Costa Rica and Panama, producing tall, slender, ringed canes topped with graceful, dark-green pinnate fronds that eventually reach 10 to 18 feet, noticeably larger and more architectural than its smaller relative C. microspadix. It thrives in the deep, humid shade beneath a tree canopy and is a good choice where a taller, jungle-like clumping palm is wanted without the size or trunk of a full landscape palm. New canes emerge continuously from the base, so a single planting fills in in a few years to form a dense green screen or backdrop planting. Protect from temperatures below the mid-20s F and keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged for best appearance.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant in very well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; young plants tolerate light shade while establishing but color and form are best in full sun, and this species is notably slower and more cold-hardy than the Gulf Coast's common Sabal palmetto.

directions: Sabal uresana is a slow-growing fan palm from the rocky canyons and foothills of Sonora, Mexico, valued for its distinctive powder-blue to silvery-gray fronds, a striking departure from the plain green of most Sabal species. Established plants have proven hardy to around 15 to 18F, making it one of the more cold-tolerant trunking Sabals available for zone 8b-9 Gulf Coast and Southwest gardens. Growth is very slow, especially before the trunk begins to form, so container specimens should be planted where their eventual 20 to 40 foot height and broad crown will not need to be worked around for many years. Once established it is highly drought tolerant and needs only sharp drainage and occasional deep watering during extended dry spells.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind, which can scorch the fine waxy leaf coating that gives this species its signature color.

directions: Trachycarpus princeps was discovered growing on cliffs above the Yarlung Tsangpo gorge in a remote part of southeastern Tibet and remains rare in cultivation despite growing interest among palm collectors. Its fan fronds are coated on the underside with a dense white to silvery-blue wax, giving the crown a striking two-toned look when the wind lifts the leaves, quite different from the plain green fronds of the more common Trachycarpus fortunei. It is a single-trunked, moderately slow-growing palm reaching 10 to 18 feet, and reports from cultivated specimens suggest cold hardiness roughly comparable to windmill palm, tolerating brief drops into the low-to-mid teens F once well established. Give it a sheltered, partly shaded spot with good drainage and consistent moisture during the growing season, and avoid exposing young plants to full, reflected summer sun.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant divisions or container clumps in rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; like other Rhapis species it grows slowly and resents soggy soil, so err on the side of underwatering rather than overwatering between waterings.

directions: Rhapis multifida is a clustering fan palm from southern China, closely related to the familiar lady palm (Rhapis excelsa) but distinguished by fronds cut into many more, noticeably narrower, finger-like segments that give the whole plant a finer, lacier texture. It forms a slowly spreading clump of slender, fiber-wrapped canes and, like its better-known relative, tolerates deep shade and low light better than almost any other palm, making it well suited to shaded courtyards, north-facing beds, or bright indoor rooms. Growth is slow, so a modest-sized clump can be used for years before it needs dividing or more space. Protect from hard freezes and give it consistently moist, fast-draining soil for the best foliage color and density.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant clumps in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in frost-free or near-frost-free climates; this species tolerates brackish soil and occasional salt spray better than most palms, making it a good choice for coastal shade gardens in the deep tropics.

directions: Licuala spinosa grows naturally along tidal mangrove margins and brackish estuaries throughout Southeast Asia, and unlike most of its Licuala relatives it forms a multi-stemmed clump rather than a single trunk, with pleated, wedge-segmented fan leaves held on spine-edged petioles. Its tolerance for wet, occasionally brackish soil and coastal salt spray sets it apart from the more delicate Licuala grandis, though it still needs the same deep, humid shade and protection from cold that all Licuala species require. Keep soil consistently moist, provide high humidity, and handle the leaf stalks carefully as the spines along their edges are sharp. Where hardy, its dense clustering habit makes it useful as a substantial shaded screen or specimen clump near water features.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online
